title: Costing and the menu
lead: What a drink costs to make, what it should sell for, and how a menu fits together.

video.title: How to Cost Out a Cocktail

read.where: A **750 ml** bottle holds about **25.4 oz**. Divide the bottle’s cost by that: a **$30** bottle is about **$1.18 an ounce**. Then cost the whole drink: every **spirit**, the **syrup**, the **citrus**, the **bitters** and the **garnish**. The small things add up.
read.mixup: A liter isn’t a fifth. A **1 L** bottle holds about **33.8 oz**.

read.bigIdea: Pour cost tells you if a drink earns its spot.
read.where: **Pour cost** is what a drink costs to make **divided by** what it sells for. A drink that costs **$2.40** and sells for **$12** has a **20%** pour cost. Bar guides put a common target at about **18–25%** for spirits and cocktails, though it varies by bar. **Over-pouring**, **spills** and **comped drinks** all raise it.
read.mixup: Pour cost isn’t profit. Rent, labor and glassware come out of the rest.

video.title: How to Determine Pricing For Beer, Liquor & Wine [Restaurant Business Plan]

keyPoints.line: it against the menu around it.

read.bigIdea: Work the price back from the cost.
read.where: Pick the **target** pour cost, then **price = cost ÷ target**. A drink costing **$2.40** at a **20%** target is **$12**. Round to a price that **fits the menu**: a new drink shouldn’t sit far above or below the drinks beside it unless there’s a reason a guest can see (a rare bottle, a bigger pour).
read.mixup: Dividing by 20, not 0.20, gives 12 cents. Use the percent as a decimal.

keyPoints.line: easy sellers, plus one to talk about.
every drink needs one a server can say.

read.bigIdea: A menu works as a set.
read.where: A good list covers the **base spirits** guests ask for, a range of **styles** (bright and shaken, strong and stirred, tall and bubbly) and a **spiritless** option. Mix **easy sellers** with one or two drinks worth **talking about**. Every drink gets a **name** a guest can say and **one line** a server can sell it with, like our menu’s sections in Lesson 3 of Level 1.
read.mixup: Eight versions of the same sour isn’t a menu. It’s one drink.
